questions.question: What does the pronoun 'hu' in 'anzalnahu' (We sent it down) refer to in the opening verse of Surah Al-Qadr?
questions.explanation: The pronoun refers to the Quran. Although the Quran is not explicitly named, it was the ongoing subject of revelation, so the listener would understand the reference immediately. This is the majority view of the Companions and Tabi'un recorded by Imam al-Tabari.

questions.question: True or false: A thousand months mentioned in verse three is approximately equal to eighty-three years and four months.
questions.explanation: A thousand months equals roughly eighty-three years and four months, which is more than a full human lifetime. The verse therefore declares that one night of sincere worship on Laylat al-Qadr surpasses the worship of an entire lifetime in divine reward.

questions.question: According to Imam al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, why is the verb 'anzala' used here rather than 'nazzala'?
options: Because 'nazzala' is reserved only for previous scriptures
Because 'anzala' indicates a single complete act of sending down, while 'nazzala' implies gradual descent
Because the two words are interchangeable with no difference in meaning
Because 'anzala' refers only to the descent of angels, not of revelation
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Abbas, explains that 'anzala' signals a single complete descent: the entire Quran was sent down on Laylat al-Qadr from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven (Bayt al-Izza), after which Jibril delivered it to the Prophet in stages over twenty-three years.

questions.question: True or false: The near-unanimous view of the Salaf, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada, is that 'al-Ruh' in verse four refers to Jibril.
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari records that the Companions and Tabi'un, including Ibn Abbas, Ibn Masud, Qatada, Mujahid, and Said ibn Jubayr, identified al-Ruh as Jibril. Ibn Kathir affirms this, noting that Jibril is mentioned separately due to his unique status as the bearer of revelation.

questions.question: How does Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran characterize the closing verse 'Peace it is until the emergence of dawn'?
options: As a warning about the dangers of staying awake too long
As a legal ruling restricting worship to the first half of the night
As one of the most beautiful endings in the Quran, bringing the reader to rest in tranquility after images of descending angels
As a metaphor with no practical implication for the believer
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb describes the verse as one of the most beautiful endings in the Quran, settling the listener into complete tranquility after the awe-inspiring scenes of descending angels and cosmic decrees. He writes that the worshipper who spends this night in devotion tastes a foretaste of the eternal salam of paradise.

questions.question: What does Wahbah al-Zuhayli emphasize about the phrase 'by the permission of their Lord' (bi-idhn rabbihim) in verse four?
options: That angels descend without any need for divine authorization
That even the highest angels can only undertake this descent through explicit divine authorization, reinforcing tawhid
That only Jibril needs permission, while other angels do not
That the permission applies only to the night of the 27th
questions.explanation: Al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir notes that this phrase contains an important theological statement: even the mightiest angels surrounding the divine throne act only by Allah's explicit authorization. This reinforces tawhid by showing that nothing in creation operates independently of divine will.

questions.question: True or false: The phrase 'wa ma adraka' in verse two is a rhetorical question of magnification (istifham ta'zimi) used to signal that what follows transcends ordinary human comprehension.
questions.explanation: Classical scholars including al-Zarkashi explain that 'wa ma adraka' is a rhetorical question of magnification, used in the Quran to introduce realities so sublime that no prior human knowledge could convey them. The effect is to create awe and anticipation before Allah Himself describes the night's value.
